structure.title: Table of Contents
structure.summary: This partial document outlines the architecture and core components of a system divided into two main modules: the State Engine and the Agent Orchestrator. The State Engine module covers its API surface (including methods like readState and writeState), internal processing layers (such as schema validation and event emission), tenant-specific configuration, multi-tiered storage strategies (using Redis, PostgreSQL, and archival storage), a detailed message processing flow, and the structure of the state object. The Agent Orchestrator module details the agent manifest system (with agent types and consumers), the trigger system for event handling, priority resolution mechanisms, a handoff manager for agent transitions, namespace enforcement for state outputs, and a summary of key technical decisions.

structure.title: Module 1: State Engine
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 1: State Engine

| Module Purpose The State Engine is the central nervous system of the entire platform. It manages session state, tracks discovery progress, accumulates context from every source (user messages, CRM data, agent outputs, background enrichment), broadcasts state changes as events to drive the reactive agent mesh, and assembles optimized context windows for LLM calls. Every other module in the platform reads from or writes to the State Engine. It is not just session management — it is the coordination backbone through which all agents communicate without direct coupling. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 1.1 API Surface
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 1.1 API Surface

The State Engine exposes five core API methods. Each serves a distinct purpose and is consumed by different parts of the platform.

nodes.title: 1.1.1 readState(sessionId, scope?)
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the function `readState(sessionId, scope?)`, which retrieves the current state of a session with varying levels of detail based on the provided `scope` parameter. It outlines different scope values—such as "full", "universal", "agent:cross-sell", "discovery", and "intent_signals"—and explains what data each returns and who typically uses them. The document emphasizes that using scoped reads instead of always returning the full state improves performance and reduces unnecessary data transfer, as different consumers (like UI components or agents) often require only specific slices of the session state.

nodes.title: 1.1.2 writeState(sessionId, patch)
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the writeState(sessionId, patch) function, which applies partial updates (patches) to a session's state by merging only the specified fields, rather than overwriting the entire state. This approach prevents data loss when multiple processes update different parts of the state concurrently, such as NLU extracting intent signals, background agents adding enrichment data, and active agents updating progress. An example patch demonstrates updating intent signals and conversation metadata without affecting other state fields.

nodes.title: 1.1.3 subscribe(sessionId, eventTypes, callback)
nodes.summary: The partial document explains the `subscribe(sessionId, eventTypes, callback)` function, which allows modules to register for notifications about specific state changes in a platform. Instead of polling for updates, modules subscribe to relevant events, enabling real-time reactivity. The document details how different subscribers (Agent Orchestrator, Conversation UI, Analytics Engine, Audit Layer) use these event notifications to trigger actions such as agent management, UI updates, analytics logging, and audit record keeping. It includes a table summarizing which events each subscriber listens to and their corresponding actions.

nodes.title: 1.1.4 assembleContext(sessionId, agentId)
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the function assembleContext(sessionId, agentId), which is designed to intelligently construct the context window for an agent’s LLM (Large Language Model) call. It addresses the challenge of providing relevant context to the LLM without exceeding token limits or including unnecessary information. The process involves five steps: reading the agent’s manifest to determine required state fields and context depth, pulling only the necessary state fields, selecting a specified depth of recent conversation history (with older messages summarized), querying a knowledge base (Foundry IQ) for relevant results, and applying a token budget to ensure the prompt stays within limits. Token allocation is fixed per context section (e.g., system prompt, customer context, conversation history, KB results, product graph, discovery progress), as defined in the agent’s manifest. Any unused tokens from one section are redistributed to others, prioritizing conversation history and KB results. The fixed allocation strategy is chosen for predictability and ease of debugging, with plans to consider more dynamic relevance scoring in the future.

nodes.title: 1.1.5 queryHistory(sessionId, filters)
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the queryHistory function, which retrieves a changelog of state changes within a single session, detailing when, what field changed, the old and new values, and who made the change. It outlines use cases such as debugging, session replay, audit/compliance, and analytics. The document also notes the decision to store this history in a PostgreSQL table (state_changelog) with relevant fields, citing simplicity and sufficiency for MVP needs, and explaining that this approach supports all identified use cases without requiring complex event sourcing.

nodes.title: 1.2 Processing Layer
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 1.2 Processing Layer

The processing layer sits between the API surface and the storage layer. Every writeState call passes through four processing stages: Schema Validation, Merge Engine, Persist, and Event Emission.

nodes.title: 1.2.1 Schema Validator
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the schema validation process for state writes in a multi-tenant system. It outlines a three-layer schema structure—Universal (platform-defined, fixed fields), Domain (tenant-specific fields and rules), and Agent (agent-specific state shapes)—each with its own validation rules and schema definitions. The document details four categories of validation performed on every write: type validation, required field validation, value constraints, and structural validation. It emphasizes that the Domain layer varies per tenant, with examples of how required fields and allowed values differ by industry. The document concludes with the decision to use JSON Schema for schema definitions, stored per tenant in a PostgreSQL table, leveraging standard validation libraries for runtime checks due to their maturity and ease of use.

nodes.title: 1.2.2 Merge Engine and Conflict Resolution
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the Merge Engine and its approach to conflict resolution when handling concurrent state updates. It explains that incoming patches are deeply merged into the existing state, updating only specified fields. To handle rare write conflicts, the system uses optimistic locking with a version number: updates succeed only if the version matches, otherwise the write fails and must be retried. The chosen strategy is justified as simple and sufficient for the current scale, avoiding the need for more complex concurrency controls like distributed locks or CRDTs.

nodes.title: 1.2.3 Event Emitter
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the Event Emitter component of a platform's state engine. It explains that after each successful state update, the engine analyzes changes and emits relevant events, enabling a reactive, state-driven architecture. The document outlines specific event mapping rules, detailing which events are emitted based on changes in state properties (e.g., detecting competitor mentions, pain points, discovery progress, workflow switches, and new recommendations). It also discusses the decision on the event transport mechanism: using an in-process Python pub/sub pattern for the MVP and switching to Redis Pub/Sub for multi-server deployments, with rationale provided for both choices.

nodes.title: 1.2.4 Context Window Builder
nodes.summary:
### 1.2.4 Context Window Builder

Responsible for assembling optimized LLM prompt contexts when agents are called. This is detailed in section 1.1.4 (assembleContext). The key technical detail: no LLM is used for context assembly in MVP. It is entirely deterministic code: read manifest requirements, pull state fields, pull conversation history (last N messages), query Foundry IQ for KB results, apply token budget via fixed section allocations.

nodes.title: 1.3.1 Schema Registry
nodes.summary: The partial document explains the role of the Schema Registry in a multi-tenant system, describing it as a PostgreSQL table that stores JSON Schema definitions for each tenant’s domain-specific state fields. It highlights the importance of the Schema Registry as the authoritative source for tenant state structure, enabling validation, configuration, and context assembly tailored to each tenant. The document provides an example schema for a tenant, illustrating how customer profile and product fields are defined. It also notes that, for the MVP, schemas are manually created during onboarding, while the full product will allow tenant admins to manage schemas through an Admin Portal UI.

nodes.title: 1.3.2 Discovery Dimensions (Tenant-Specific Progress Model)
nodes.summary:
This partial document section explains the concept of "discovery dimensions" within a tenant-specific progress model for AI-driven recommendation systems. It outlines how each business (tenant) defines its own discovery dimensions—key pieces of information an AI agent must gather before making high-quality recommendations. The document details three main functions of discovery dimensions: guiding the AI's adaptive questioning, gating recommendations until enough context is collected, and visually tracking progress via a weighted progress bar in the UI.

A comparative table illustrates how discovery dimensions differ between industries (e.g., IT Reseller vs. Insurance Brokerage), showing that each dimension has a unique weight, method of completion (e.g., auto-fill, conversation), and threshold for unlocking recommendations. The document also specifies the structure of each dimension (ID, label, weight, status, method of completion, and suggested questions) and explains how overall progress is calculated as a weighted sum based on the completion status of each dimension.

nodes.title: 1.4.1 Redis Cache (Hot Storage)
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the use of Redis as a hot storage cache for managing active session state in a chat application. It details that Redis holds the full current state object for each active session to enable rapid read/write operations during conversations, significantly reducing latency compared to PostgreSQL. The document specifies what data is stored in Redis (session state and subscriber registry) and what is not (conversation history, state changelogs, and closed sessions), clarifying that Redis is used for fast, temporary storage while PostgreSQL handles larger or persistent data.

nodes.title: 1.4.2 PostgreSQL (Warm Storage)
nodes.summary:
### 1.4.2 PostgreSQL (Warm Storage)

PostgreSQL is the durable store for ALL session data. Even while a session is active in Redis, every write also goes to PostgreSQL (write-through pattern). Tables:

sessions: Session metadata — id, tenant_id, rep_id, customer_id, status, created_at, ended_at.

session_state: Full state JSON per session, updated on every write.

conversation_messages: Every message with role, content, timestamp, extracted entities.

state_changelog: Every state mutation with field_changed, old_value, new_value, source, timestamp.

feedback_signals: Accept, dismiss, usage events for the Feedback Engine.

nodes.title: 1.4.3 Cold Archive (Full Product Only)
nodes.summary:
### 1.4.3 Cold Archive (Full Product Only)

Sessions older than 6-12 months are archived to Azure Blob Storage as compressed JSON. Summary records remain in PostgreSQL for long-term analytics. For MVP, only Redis + PostgreSQL are needed. Cold archival is a full-product concern when data volume warrants it.

nodes.title: 1.5 Exact Message Processing Flow
nodes.summary: The partial document details the exact processing flow for handling a message sent by a representative in a conversation system. It outlines each step from message receipt to event broadcasting and subscriber reactions, emphasizing that the pipeline is deterministic and fast, with only a single, focused LLM (GPT-4o-mini) call for NLU extraction. The steps include session validation, NLU extraction for structured data, state patch construction, schema validation, state merging, persistence to databases, event emission, subscriber reactions, and conditional context assembly for agent calls. The document highlights the minimal use of AI, ensuring predictability and speed, and describes the specific data extracted and actions triggered at each stage.

nodes.title: 1.6 Complete State Object Shape
nodes.summary: This partial document provides a comprehensive reference for the runtime JSON structure of a session state object in a software system. It details each section of the state object, specifying which system component writes to each field and when. The main sections include metadata (session identifiers, versioning, timestamps), session status (workflow, agents, message count), customer information (profile and products), intent signals (detected by NLU), discovery progress, agent-specific state, UI state, and conversation details. Additionally, the document explains the rationale behind the three-layer state schema design—comprising Universal (fixed, platform-wide), Domain (tenant-configured), and Agent-Specific (per-agent namespace) layers—stored in PostgreSQL using JSONB columns for flexibility and isolation. This structure ensures both standardization and extensibility, allowing agents to manage their own state without interfering with others.

structure.title: Module 2: Agent Orchestrator
structure.prefix_summary:
# Module 2: Agent Orchestrator

| Module Purpose The Agent Orchestrator is the traffic controller of the platform. It decides WHEN agents should activate, WHICH agent takes priority when multiple trigger simultaneously, HOW to handle transitions between core workflow agents, and WHERE to route agent outputs. It contains zero AI — it is entirely deterministic, rule-based logic. The LLMs are only involved when the actual agents execute (Modules 6-12). The Orchestrator is pure traffic control executing in sub-millisecond time. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 2.1 Agent Manifest System
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 2.1 Agent Manifest System

Every agent in the platform registers itself via a manifest — a declarative document that tells the Orchestrator everything it needs to know about the agent without the Orchestrator understanding the agent’s internal logic. Think of it as a job application: the agent declares who it is, what it needs, when it should be called, and what it will produce.

nodes.title: 2.1.1 Manifest Fields and Who Consumes Them
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the key fields present in an agent manifest, describing the purpose of each field and which system component consumes it. It details how fields like agent identity, triggers, required state fields, conversation history depth, knowledge base context needs, output namespaces, merge strategies, priority, core workflow status, and discovery configuration are used by various subsystems such as the Agent Registry, Trigger Evaluator, Context Assembler, Schema Validator, Merge Engine, Priority Resolver, Handoff Manager, and Discovery initialization. The table provides a clear mapping between manifest fields, their roles, and the internal modules responsible for processing them.

nodes.title: 2.1.2 The Four Agent Types
nodes.summary:
This partial document section describes the four types of agents used in an orchestrated system, detailing their execution behaviors and how the Orchestrator manages them based on the agent type specified in the manifest. The agent types are:

1. CORE_WORKFLOW: Executes exclusively, with only one active at a time, driving the main conversation and interacting directly in the chat. It receives the full context and is used for primary flows like Cross-Sell or Upsell.
2. PLUGIN_QUICK_ACTION: Executes lazily, appearing as a UI button that only runs when explicitly triggered by the user. Its results are shown outside the main chat, and it uses a smaller context.
3. BACKGROUND_ENRICHMENT: Executes silently and immediately in the background, with no user visibility. Its results are stored for use by other agents, requiring minimal context.
4. REACTIVE_SUGGESTION: Proactively surfaces suggestions in the UI based on signals, which can be accepted or dismissed by the user. Unlike plugins, these are not user-invoked but system-suggested.

The section provides examples for each agent type and explains how their execution and UI presentation differ.

nodes.title: 2.2.1 Trigger Conditions Deep Dive
nodes.summary: This partial document section provides a detailed explanation of trigger conditions within a manifest for a reactive agent mesh. It describes the structure of a trigger block, which includes conditions, a conditionType, and a combineWith directive. The document outlines different condition types—state_match (evaluates current state), always (unconditional triggers), event_match (triggers on specific events), and composite (combines state and event logic). It explains how the combineWith directive determines whether multiple conditions within a block are evaluated with AND (all must be true) or OR (any can be true). Additionally, it clarifies that between separate trigger blocks, the relationship is always OR, meaning any satisfied block will activate the agent. Examples are provided to illustrate each concept.

nodes.title: 2.2.2 Complete Operator Reference
nodes.summary: This partial document provides a comprehensive reference for the supported operators used in condition statements. It details each operator’s name, its meaning, applicable data types, and example usage. The operators cover equality and inequality checks, numeric comparisons, array length checks, substring or element containment, existence checks, set membership, and regular expression matching. The table format clarifies how each operator functions and the types of data they can be applied to, serving as a guide for constructing conditional logic based on state field values.

nodes.title: 2.2.3 Tenant Trigger Overrides
nodes.summary:
### 2.2.3 Tenant Trigger Overrides

Every agent has default trigger conditions defined in its manifest. Tenant overrides allow modification of these defaults without changing agent code. Three override types exist:

disable: Completely turns off an agent for this tenant. Example: Insurance brokerage disables Competitor Card because regulations prevent showing carrier comparisons.

replace_trigger: Replaces the agent’s default trigger with entirely new conditions. Example: SaaS company replaces Cross-Sell’s auto-activate trigger with one that requires 5+ messages first, so reps can build rapport before the agent activates.

add_trigger: Adds additional conditions that must ALSO be met (AND logic with the default). Example: Medical distributor adds "customer annual spend must be >= $100K" to the Upsell agent’s trigger, restricting upsell to high-value accounts.

For MVP: Overrides are hardcoded JSON per tenant, set during onboarding. For full product: configurable in the Admin Portal.

nodes.title: 2.3 Priority Resolution
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the process of priority resolution when multiple agents are triggered simultaneously in a system. It outlines a cascade of tiebreakers used by the Priority Resolver to determine the order in which agents are surfaced or executed. The main points include: separating agents by type (core workflows, plugins, background, and reactive agents), using a priority enumeration (CRITICAL to BACKGROUND), evaluating trigger specificity (number of matched conditions), considering signal strength (number of intent signals), and applying a hardcoded, tenant-configurable preference order as the final tiebreaker. The document also clarifies that multiple agents can share the same priority, and losing core agents are not discarded but offered as alternative suggestions to the user.

nodes.title: 2.4 Handoff Manager
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 2.4 Handoff Manager

The Handoff Manager handles transitions between core workflow agents. This is fundamentally different from simple activation because it involves suspending one agent, transferring context, switching discovery dimensions, and enabling future resume.

nodes.title: 2.4.1 Handoff Confidence Scoring
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the "Handoff Confidence Scoring" mechanism used by a Handoff Manager to determine when to switch between core agents during an active session. It outlines a confidence scoring system based on three factors: the number of intent signals, the progress of the current agent (discovery depth), and the presence of explicit keywords. Depending on the calculated confidence score, the system will either automatically switch agents, suggest a switch to the user, or ignore the signal. Manual agent switches by the user always trigger an immediate switch. The document provides a table summarizing the actions taken at different confidence score ranges and the rationale behind each action.

nodes.title: 2.4.2 The Five Atomic Handoff Operations
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the five atomic operations involved in an agent handoff process. It details how the current agent is suspended, preserving its state and discovery dimensions; how context is transferred to the new agent; how discovery dimensions are switched and initialized for the new agent; how the new agent is activated within the workflow; and how the user interface is updated to reflect the change, including workflow progress and quick actions. Each operation is atomic, ensuring rollback if any step fails.

nodes.title: 2.4.3 Discovery Dimension Auto-Fill During Handoff
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains how discovery dimensions for a new agent are automatically populated during handoff or activation. It details that there is no direct mapping between agents; instead, each agent independently specifies where to source its initial data using the auto_fill_from configuration. Each auto_fill_from entry defines the state path to read from, a transformation function to process the data, and a status indicating whether the auto-fill is considered "complete" or "partial." Multiple sources can be listed and are tried in order. The approach ensures agents are self-contained and only interact with the shared state, allowing new agents to be added without modifying others.

nodes.title: 2.4.4 Discovery Dimension Preservation
nodes.summary:
### 2.4.4 Discovery Dimension Preservation

When discovery dimensions switch during handoff, the previous agent’s dimensions are NOT deleted. They are preserved inside the suspended agent’s state namespace:

The top-level discovery object always reflects the ACTIVE agent’s dimensions. This is what the UI reads for the progress bar and what the Orchestrator reads for threshold checks.

Each suspended agent’s dimensions live in agent_state.{agentId}._suspended_discovery. When that agent is resumed, the Handoff Manager copies _suspended_discovery back into the top-level discovery object, restoring the agent’s progress exactly where it was suspended.

Additionally, any intelligence learned during the time the agent was suspended (from the agent that was active in between) gets added as inherited_post_suspension context. The resumed agent benefits from everything that happened while it was dormant.

nodes.title: 2.5 StateOutputs.namespace — Write Boundary Enforcement
nodes.summary: This partial document explains the role of the namespace field in stateOutputs as a mechanism for enforcing write boundaries in a system with multiple agents and plugins. It details how each agent declares which parts of the state it can modify, and how the Schema Validator ensures agents cannot write outside their assigned namespaces, preventing data corruption and unauthorized overwrites. The document provides a table listing specific write permissions and restrictions for various agents and plugins. It also describes the mergeStrategy options (deep_merge and replace) that control how state updates are applied within each namespace.

nodes.title: 2.6 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary: This partial document summarizes key technical decisions for an Agent Orchestrator platform. The main points include: (1) The orchestrator operates entirely on deterministic, rule-based logic without using large language models (LLMs), ensuring fast and predictable core routing, while LLMs are used only within individual agents. (2) Agent capabilities and requirements are registered via static manifest documents, making the system transparent, inspectable, and easier to debug, especially with many agents. (3) Handoffs between agents are suggested rather than forced when system confidence is moderate, preserving user control and minimizing workflow disruption. (4) Each agent independently specifies how to auto-fill its discovery dimensions from shared state paths, avoiding tight coupling between agents and using the shared state as the integration layer.
